why: SQL is the most requested skill across data, BA and support roles. Interviews almost always include a live query exercise.
outcome: write SELECT queries with filters, joins, aggregations, CTEs and window functions, and explain what they return.

lessons.title: Read data: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY
text: A table is a set of rows with named columns. SELECT chooses columns, FROM chooses the table, WHERE keeps only the rows that match a condition, ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT keeps the first rows.
SQL is written in that order but executed in another one: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. This explains why you cannot use a column alias in WHERE.
points: Text values use single quotes: 'Paris'.
NULL means unknown: test it with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, never = NULL.
Combine conditions with AND / OR and use parentheses to be explicit.
IN ('a','b') and BETWEEN 10 AND 20 keep queries short; LIKE 'Data%' matches a prefix.

example.code:
SELECT first_name, city, salary
FROM employees
WHERE city IN ('Paris', 'Lyon')
  AND salary >= 40000
  AND manager_id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 10;
example.note: Top 10 salaries in Paris or Lyon, among people who have a manager.

lessons.title: Summarise: GROUP BY, aggregates, HAVING
text: Aggregate functions turn many rows into one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. With GROUP BY you get one result row per group.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after the aggregate is computed.
points: Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated.
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) ignores NULLs; COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts unique values.
Use ROUND(AVG(x), 2) to present clean numbers.

example.code:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount, ROUND(AVG(salary), 0) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE hired_on >= '2023-01-01'
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;
example.note: Departments with at least 5 people hired since 2023, by average salary.

lessons.title: Combine tables: JOINs
text: A JOIN matches rows of two tables on a condition, usually a foreign key equal to a primary key (orders.customer_id = customers.id).
INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows. LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table and fills the right side with NULL when nothing matches; that is how you find what is missing.
points: Always alias tables (o, c) and prefix columns: o.amount, c.name.
Check row counts before and after a join: a join on a non-unique key multiplies rows.
LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL finds rows with no match (customers without orders).

example.code:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
example.note: Customers without orders still appear, with 0 orders and 0 revenue.

lessons.title: Go further: CTEs and window functions
text: A CTE (WITH name AS (...)) names an intermediate result so a long query reads top to bottom.
Window functions compute a value per row while looking at other rows, without collapsing them: rankings, running totals, the previous value. They are the classic intermediate interview question.
points: ROW_NUMBER() gives 1, 2, 3; RANK() leaves gaps after ties; DENSE_RANK() does not.
PARTITION BY restarts the calculation for each group; ORDER BY inside OVER sets the order.
LAG(x) / LEAD(x) read the previous / next row: perfect for month-over-month changes.
SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY day) gives a running total.

example.code:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', ordered_at) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change_vs_prev
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
example.note: DATE_TRUNC is PostgreSQL / Snowflake / BigQuery-style; SQL Server uses DATETRUNC or FORMAT.

lessons.title: Performance: indexes and query plans
text: A query that takes seconds on a big table usually reads every row. An index is a sorted copy of one or more columns with pointers to the rows, like the index of a book: the database jumps to the right rows instead of scanning everything.

EXPLAIN shows the plan the database chose; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows real timings. Look for full scans (Seq Scan) on large tables, row estimates far from reality and sorts or joins that spill to disk.
points: Index the columns you filter and join on most; put the most selective, equality-filtered column first.
Functions on a column (WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026) prevent using its index: filter on a range instead.
Every index speeds up reads but slows down writes and takes space: do not index everything.
Select only the columns you need instead of SELECT * on wide tables.

example.note: Measure before and after: the plan, not intuition, tells you what changed.

lessons.title: Subqueries, CTEs and recursive CTEs
text: A subquery is a query inside another one. It can return a single value (a scalar subquery in SELECT or WHERE), a list (WHERE id IN (SELECT ...)) or a whole table (FROM (SELECT ...) AS t). A correlated subquery refers to the outer row, for example the average salary of the current employee's department: conceptually it is evaluated once per outer row, which can be slow on large tables if the optimizer cannot rewrite it as a join.

A CTE does the same job but gives the intermediate result a name, so multi-step logic reads from top to bottom and the same step can be referenced twice. Since PostgreSQL 12, a CTE used once is usually inlined like a subquery, so it is not slower; WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (...) forces it to be computed once. Choose by readability: a short filter fits in a subquery, three or more steps belong in CTEs.

EXISTS and NOT EXISTS check whether at least one matching row exists and stop at the first match. Prefer NOT EXISTS to NOT IN: if the subquery returns a single NULL, x NOT IN (...) is never true and the query silently returns nothing.

A recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE) walks hierarchies such as org charts, category trees or bills of materials. An anchor query returns the starting rows, then a recursive part joins back to the CTE and adds rows until a step returns nothing new. SQL Server writes the same query without the RECURSIVE keyword; Oracle also offers CONNECT BY.
points: A scalar subquery must return at most one row, otherwise the query fails.
Give every derived table an alias: FROM (SELECT ...) AS t (required by most databases).
Use NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN when the subquery column can be NULL.
Use UNION ALL in a recursive CTE and add a depth limit to stop on cyclic data.
Recursive CTEs can also generate rows (a list of dates), but PostgreSQL's generate_series is simpler for that.

example.code:
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, first_name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM employees
  WHERE manager_id IS NULL              -- anchor: the top of the org chart
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.first_name, e.manager_id, c.depth + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id   -- recursive step: direct reports
  WHERE c.depth < 10                    -- safety stop
)
SELECT depth, first_name
FROM chain
ORDER BY depth, first_name;
example.note: Each level of the org chart is added until no new employee is found.

lessons.title: Window functions in depth: frames, running totals and ties
text: OVER has three parts: PARTITION BY (which rows belong together), ORDER BY (in which order) and the frame (which rows around the current one are used). Ranking functions and LAG / LEAD only use the first two; aggregates such as SUM or AVG over a window also use the frame.

The default frame is a classic trap. With ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the database uses RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. RANGE treats rows with the same ORDER BY value as peers, so two orders on the same day get the same running total. Write ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a strict row-by-row total, and ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a 7-row moving average.

Decide explicitly how to handle ties. ROW_NUMBER picks an arbitrary order among ties unless ORDER BY ends with a unique column (ORDER BY amount DESC, id). For a top 3 per group that keeps ties, filter on DENSE_RANK() <= 3. NTILE(4) splits rows into quartiles. FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE return the edges of the frame, which is why LAST_VALUE with the default frame returns the current row.

Window functions are computed after WHERE, so you cannot filter on them directly: compute them in a CTE and filter outside. Snowflake, BigQuery and Databricks add QUALIFY for this; PostgreSQL does not.
points: LAG(x, 1, 0) takes an offset and a default for the first row.
SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g) without ORDER BY gives the group total: x / that total is a share.
WINDOW w AS (...) names a window definition you can reuse (PostgreSQL, MySQL 8).
A 7-row average is a 7-day average only if every day has a row: fill gaps first.

example.code:
SELECT store_id, order_day, revenue,
       SUM(revenue) OVER w_running AS running_total,
       ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY order_day
             ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg_7_rows,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY order_day) AS change_vs_prev
FROM daily_sales
WINDOW w_running AS (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY order_day
                     ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
ORDER BY store_id, order_day;
example.note: daily_sales has one row per store and day; revenue is numeric.

lessons.title: NULLs, three-valued logic and data cleaning
text: In SQL a condition is TRUE, FALSE or UNKNOWN. Any comparison with NULL (NULL = NULL, status <> 'cancelled' when status is NULL) is UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. So WHERE status <> 'cancelled' silently drops the rows where status is NULL, and NOT (UNKNOWN) is still UNKNOWN. Aggregates skip NULLs, except COUNT(*): AVG(bonus) averages only the people who have a bonus.

A few functions make NULLs explicit. COALESCE(a, b, c) returns the first non-NULL value. NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a equals b, the standard way to avoid a division by zero: revenue / NULLIF(visits, 0). a IS DISTINCT FROM b compares values while treating two NULLs as equal. In PostgreSQL, NULLs sort last in ascending order and first in descending order; NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST makes it explicit (MySQL and SQL Server do not support this syntax).

Data cleaning in SQL relies on the same small toolbox: CASE WHEN to map messy values to clean categories, TRIM, LOWER, REPLACE and SPLIT_PART to normalise text, CAST(x AS DATE) or x::date to convert types, DATE_TRUNC, EXTRACT and intervals (created_at + INTERVAL '7 days') for dates. One value that cannot be cast makes the whole query fail, so filter or fix bad values first (SQL Server has TRY_CAST, PostgreSQL does not).
Keep the raw table untouched and put cleaning rules in a view or a new table: you can rerun them, explain every rule and compare before and after.
points: WHERE status <> 'x' OR status IS NULL keeps NULL rows on purpose.
NULL in arithmetic or || concatenation makes the result NULL; CONCAT() skips NULLs.
COUNT(*) - COUNT(col) is the number of NULLs in col.
COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE col IS NULL) is a PostgreSQL shortcut for SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).

example.code:
CREATE VIEW customers_clean AS
SELECT
  id,
  INITCAP(TRIM(city)) AS city,
  LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS email,
  CASE
    WHEN LOWER(TRIM(status)) IN ('active', 'actif') THEN 'active'
    WHEN status IS NULL OR TRIM(status) = '' THEN 'unknown'
    ELSE 'inactive'
  END AS status,
  COALESCE(phone, 'n/a') AS phone,
  ROUND(revenue::numeric / NULLIF(orders, 0), 2) AS avg_basket,
  signup_at::date AS signup_day
FROM raw_customers;
example.note: INITCAP and the :: cast are PostgreSQL; elsewhere use CAST(x AS DATE) and your database's text functions.

lessons.title: Transactions and isolation basics
text: A transaction groups statements that must succeed or fail together: BEGIN, the statements, then COMMIT to keep the changes or ROLLBACK to cancel them. This is the A of ACID (atomicity): a money transfer must never debit one account without crediting the other. In PostgreSQL a statement outside BEGIN runs in its own transaction and is committed immediately (autocommit). Check your SQL client's setting: some tools open a transaction for you and keep locks until you commit.

Isolation controls what a transaction sees of the others running at the same time. The standard levels are READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE; each one prevents more anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom rows). READ COMMITTED is the default in PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle, REPEATABLE READ in MySQL InnoDB. PostgreSQL never shows uncommitted data, even in READ UNCOMMITTED. Under SERIALIZABLE, PostgreSQL may abort a transaction with a serialization failure that the application must retry.

Writes lock the rows they change until the transaction ends. A long transaction blocks other writers and, in PostgreSQL, prevents old row versions from being cleaned up. Keep transactions short and never wait for user input inside one. To avoid a lost update (two sessions read the same value, both write), update in a single statement (SET stock = stock - 1) or lock the rows first with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
points: In PostgreSQL an error inside a transaction aborts it: every next statement fails until ROLLBACK.
SAVEPOINT s and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s undo part of a transaction.
DDL is transactional in PostgreSQL (a CREATE TABLE can be rolled back), not in MySQL or Oracle.
Check how many rows each UPDATE touched before you COMMIT.

example.note: Other sessions see either all three changes or none of them.

lessons.title: Change data safely: INSERT ... SELECT, UPDATE with joins, upserts
text: Writing data is where SQL mistakes become expensive. Before any UPDATE or DELETE, run the same WHERE clause as a SELECT COUNT(*) and check the number. Work inside a transaction so you can roll back, and in PostgreSQL add RETURNING to see the rows you changed (SQL Server uses OUTPUT). An UPDATE without WHERE changes every row of the table.

INSERT INTO target (cols) SELECT ... copies the result of a query; always list the columns so a new column or a different order cannot shift values. To update from another table, PostgreSQL writes UPDATE t SET ... FROM s WHERE t.id = s.id, SQL Server UPDATE t SET ... FROM t JOIN s ON ..., MySQL UPDATE t JOIN s ON ... SET .... If the source has several rows per target row, the result is unpredictable: deduplicate the source first. PostgreSQL deletes with a join using DELETE FROM t USING s WHERE ....

An upsert inserts new rows and updates existing ones. PostgreSQL uses INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col, which needs a unique constraint or index on the key; MySQL has INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE. The standard MERGE INTO target USING source ON ... WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT exists in PostgreSQL 15+, SQL Server, Oracle, Snowflake and BigQuery. Upserts make loads idempotent: rerunning the same load does not create duplicates.
points: Run the WHERE as a SELECT first, then the UPDATE or DELETE inside BEGIN.
Delete or update millions of rows in batches to keep locks and logs small.
TRUNCATE empties a whole table instantly: it is never a replacement for DELETE ... WHERE.
A load that can safely run twice is worth more than a fast one that cannot.

example.code:
-- Load staging rows into customers; safe to run again
BEGIN;

INSERT INTO customers (id, email, city, updated_at)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (id) id, LOWER(TRIM(email)), city, loaded_at
FROM staging_customers
ORDER BY id, loaded_at DESC
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE
SET email = EXCLUDED.email,
    city = EXCLUDED.city,
    updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at
WHERE customers.updated_at < EXCLUDED.updated_at
RETURNING id;

COMMIT;
example.note: DISTINCT ON (PostgreSQL) keeps the latest staging row per id: without it, two rows with the same id make ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE fail.

items: First n rows (SQL Server: TOP n)
Matches any value in the list
a JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id
All rows of a, NULL when no match
Rows of a with no match in b
CASE WHEN x THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY d)
Filter on a list from another query
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE ...)
Rows with no match, safe with NULLs
WITH RECURSIVE t AS (anchor UNION ALL step)
Walk a hierarchy level by level
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
NULL when a = 0: avoids division by zero
Comparison that treats two NULLs as equal
Lock the rows you are about to update
UPDATE t SET c = s.c FROM s WHERE t.id = s.id
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET c = EXCLUDED.c
MERGE INTO t USING s ON ... WHEN MATCHED THEN ...
Show the rows changed (SQL Server: OUTPUT)

pitfalls: Writing = NULL instead of IS NULL: the condition is never true.
Putting a condition on the right table of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE, which silently turns it into an INNER JOIN. Put it in the ON clause instead.
Joining on a key that is not unique and getting duplicated totals.
Using SELECT * in production queries: slower and breaks when columns change.
Using NOT IN with a subquery that can return NULL: the query returns no rows at all. Use NOT EXISTS.
Relying on the default window frame for a running total: with RANGE, rows sharing the same ORDER BY value get the same total. Write ROWS BETWEEN ... and add a unique tie-breaker.
Running an UPDATE or DELETE outside a transaction without first checking its WHERE with a SELECT: one typo can change the whole table.

exercises.q: List the 5 cities with the most customers, with the number of customers.
exercises.hint: GROUP BY city, ORDER BY the count, LIMIT.
exercises.answer:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY customers DESC
LIMIT 5;

exercises.q: Find customers who never placed an order.
exercises.hint: LEFT JOIN and look for NULL on the orders side.
exercises.answer:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

exercises.q: For each customer, return their most recent order only.
exercises.hint: ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by customer, ordered by date descending.

exercises.q: Rewrite this filter so an index on created_at can be used: WHERE EXTRACT(MONTH FROM created_at) = 1 AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at) = 2026.
exercises.hint: Compare the column itself to a date range.
exercises.answer:
SELECT id, total
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01'
  AND created_at <  '2026-02-01';

exercises.q: List the employees who earn more than the average salary of their own department.
exercises.hint: A correlated subquery that compares with the department of the outer row.
exercises.answer:
SELECT e.first_name, e.department, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
  SELECT AVG(e2.salary)
  FROM employees e2
  WHERE e2.department = e.department
);

exercises.q: Show each order with a running total of amount per customer, strictly row by row even when two orders share a date.
exercises.hint: An explicit ROWS frame and a unique tie-breaker in ORDER BY.
exercises.answer:
SELECT customer_id, ordered_at, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at, id
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id, ordered_at, id;

exercises.q: Compute the conversion rate (conversions / clicks, in %) per campaign without failing when a campaign has 0 clicks.
exercises.hint: NULLIF on the divisor, and multiply by 100.0 to avoid integer division.
exercises.answer:
SELECT campaign,
       SUM(clicks) AS clicks,
       SUM(conversions) AS conversions,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(conversions) / NULLIF(SUM(clicks), 0), 1) AS conversion_pct
FROM campaign_stats
GROUP BY campaign;

exercises.q: Load the prices of staging_prices (one row per sku) into products: insert new skus, update the price of existing ones.
exercises.hint: INSERT ... SELECT with ON CONFLICT; products needs a unique constraint on sku.
exercises.answer:
INSERT INTO products (sku, price, updated_at)
SELECT sku, price, NOW()
FROM staging_prices
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE
SET price = EXCLUDED.price,
    updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at;

interview.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
interview.a: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and is where conditions on COUNT, SUM, etc. go.

INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row of the left table, with NULLs for the right table when there is no match. Use LEFT JOIN when you must not lose rows, for example customers without orders.

All number rows within a window. ROW_NUMBER is always 1, 2, 3 even with ties. RANK gives ties the same number and skips the next ones (1, 1, 3). DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without gaps (1, 1, 2).

interview.q: A query became slow in production. How do you investigate?
interview.a: I reproduce it with EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see the plan and where the time goes, check whether the data volume or the plan changed, and look for full scans, bad row estimates or missing indexes. Then I fix the cause: add or adjust an index, rewrite a non-sargable filter, update statistics or reduce the columns and rows read, and compare the plan before and after.

interview.q: Subquery or CTE: which one do you use and why?
interview.a: They can express the same logic, and modern optimizers such as PostgreSQL 12+ usually inline a CTE used once, so the choice is mostly about readability. I use a subquery for a short, one-off filter and CTEs as soon as the logic has several steps or reuses an intermediate result. For hierarchies I need a recursive CTE, which a subquery cannot do.

interview.q: What happens when a WHERE condition meets a NULL?
interview.a: SQL uses three-valued logic: a comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. So status <> 'cancelled' drops rows where status is NULL, and NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns nothing. I test NULLs explicitly with IS NULL, use COALESCE or IS DISTINCT FROM, and check NULL counts when I profile a table.

They define what a transaction sees of concurrent changes. READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE prevent progressively more anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms. Higher levels are safer but cause more waiting or retries. READ COMMITTED is the default in PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle; under SERIALIZABLE the application must be ready to retry failed transactions.

interview.q: How do you make a data load safe to run twice?
interview.a: I make it idempotent: load into a staging table, deduplicate it, then upsert into the target on its business key with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT or MERGE, or replace a whole partition (delete the day, insert the day) inside one transaction. Rerunning the same load then gives the same result instead of duplicates, which makes retries and backfills safe.
